title: Frequency Map Analysis for Alternating Elements
approach_explanation: The problem asks whether we can permute an array such that every adjacent pair sums to the same constant $k$. This condition implies that elements at alternating positions must be equal ($b_1 = b_3 = b_5 = 	ext{...}$ and $b_2 = b_4 = b_6 = 	ext{...}$). Thus, the array can contain at most two distinct values. If there is only 1 distinct value, we can always arrange them to be good. If there are exactly 2 distinct values, they must alternate (e.g., $x, y, x, y, 	ext{...}$), which means their frequencies must differ by at most $1$. If there are more than 2 distinct values, it is impossible to satisfy the condition.

code_breakdown.explanation: Read the number of test cases $t$, and for each test case, read the array size $n$ and populate a frequency map of the elements using `std::map`.
Check if the number of distinct elements (`freq.size()`) is strictly greater than 2. If so, it's impossible to form the alternating sum property, and we output "No".
If there is only 1 distinct element, all adjacent sums are identical, so we immediately output "Yes".
If there are exactly 2 distinct elements, we extract their frequencies and compute their absolute difference. If the difference is $\le 1$, we output "Yes"; otherwise, we output "No".

complexity_analysis.time_justification: Inserting $n$ elements into a `std::map` takes $O(n \log n)$ time per test case because each insertion requires logarithmic time relative to the number of distinct elements. Across $t$ test cases, the total time complexity is $O(\sum n \log n)$.
complexity_analysis.space_justification: In the worst case, all $n$ elements in the array are distinct, meaning the `std::map` stores up to $n$ key-value pairs, requiring $O(n)$ auxiliary space.

strengths: Clean and concise implementation of the core logic.
Accurately handles all theoretical cases (1 distinct element, 2 distinct elements, and >2 distinct elements).
edge_cases_handled: Arrays with all identical elements ($n$ distinct count = 1).
Arrays with exactly two distinct elements with balanced or slightly unbalanced frequencies.
Arrays with more than 2 distinct elements.
best_practices_feedback: Prefer `std::unordered_map` for an average $O(1)$ lookup and insertion time instead of `std::map`, improving time complexity to $O(n)$.

optimization_and_alternatives.tradeoffs: Replacing `std::map` with `std::unordered_map` reduces the time complexity from $O(n \log n)$ to expected $O(n)$ by utilizing a hash table instead of a balanced binary search tree.
Sort the array and check counts of the first and last elements to avoid map overhead, keeping auxiliary space minimal.
